content: An oxidizing agent, also referred to as an oxidant or oxidizer, can be defined in two primary ways: 1. A chemical compound that readily transfers oxygen atoms to another substance. 2. A substance that gains electrons during a redox (reduction-oxidation) chemical reaction. The first definition is more commonly used by organic chemists, while the second is more general. In both cases, the oxidizing agent itself becomes reduced during the process. To simplify: The oxidizing agent is reduced (it gains electrons). The reducing agent is oxidized (it loses electrons). Every atom in a molecule can be assigned an oxidation number, which changes when an oxidizing agent acts on a substrate. Redox reactions occur when electrons are exchanged between substances. A helpful mnemonic to remember this is OIL RIG (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons) or LEO the lion says GER (Lose Electrons: Oxidation, Gain Electrons: Reduction). Example of Oxidation: Formation of Iron(III) Oxide In the reaction forming iron(III) oxide: The oxidation number of iron (Fe) starts at 0 and increases to +3 after the reaction. The oxidation number of oxygen (O) starts at 0 and decreases to -2. This can be broken down into two half-reactions: Oxidation Half-Reaction: Fe⁰ → Fe³⁺ + 3e⁻ Reduction Half-Reaction: O₂ + 4e⁻ → 2O²⁻ In this reaction: Iron (Fe) is oxidized because its oxidation number increases. It acts as the reducing agent because it donates electrons to oxygen. Oxygen (O) is reduced because its oxidation number decreases. It acts as the oxidizing agent because it accepts electrons from iron. Alternate Meanings of Oxidizing Agents The term oxidizing agent has acquired multiple meanings due to the widespread nature of oxidation processes (e.g., in explosives, chemical synthesis, and corrosion). 1. In one context, an oxidizing agent is a substance that accepts electrons from another reagent. In this case, it is also called an electron acceptor. A classic example is the ferrocenium ion (Fe(C₅H₅)₂⁺), which accepts an electron to form ferrocene (Fe(C₅H₅)₂). 2. In another context, an oxidizing agent transfers oxygen atoms to a substrate. Here, it may be referred to as an oxygenation reagent or oxygen-atom transfer agent. Examples include permanganate (MnO₄⁻), chromate (CrO₄²⁻), osmium tetroxide (OsO₄), and perchlorate (ClO₄⁻). These species are all oxides, often polyoxides, and in some cases, they can also act as electron acceptors (e.g., the conversion of permanganate to manganate). Dangerous Goods Definition of Oxidizing Agents According to the Australian Dangerous Goods Code (6th Edition), an oxidizing agent is defined as a substance that, while not necessarily combustible itself, can cause or contribute to the combustion of other materials, typically by yielding oxygen. By this definition, some materials classified as oxidizing agents by analytical chemists may not be considered oxidizing agents in the context of dangerous goods. For example, potassium dichromate does not meet the dangerous goods criteria for an oxidizing agent.
